newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ford, unveiling Puma, sees booming small cars.
newsitem.headline: Ford, unveiling Puma, sees booming small cars.

text.p: Small car sales in Europe are on the rise and will account for 35 percent of the market by 2000, Ford Motor Co of Europe said on Tuesday.
"Small car sales now account for 32 percent of sales in western Europe, and will hit 35 percent by the end of the century," Ford of Europe chairman Jacques Nasser said.
Car sales in western Europe totalled 12.8 million in 1996.

Nasser was unveiling Ford's new small coupe, the Puma, based on the little Fiesta. The Puma has a 1.7 litre, four cylinder engine. The Puma would compete in a segment which includes the Opel Tigra, introduced more than a year ago by General Motors Corp Europe.
Nasser, said Ford spent just over $66 million developing the Puma, which he said was aimed at a new category of motorists seeking more performance and individuality.
"I gave them $66 million to develop the Puma, and they ran overbudget by a smidgeon," Nasser told a press conference at the Geneva Car Show.
Nasser said Ford, with products like the tiny Ka which is smaller than the Fiesta, was aiming to cover more specialised market niches.
Some analysts say this is a dangerous ploy for manufacturers because buyers often buy a cheaper, smaller variant and not the bigger, more expensive and more profitable cars.
Others say Ford has missed the boat in this category, and wonder if the Puma's striking looks will appeal to the public.
"The Ford Puma could be a stillbirth," said Peter Schmidt, joint managing director of Britain's Automotive Industy Data.

"It looks like a cross between a Fiat Coupe and the rear looks like an Opel Tigra. This sector is performing attrociously. When it was conceived the market looked good. But this type of product like the Tigra, went through the roof then collapsed," Schmidt said,
"Ford has a potential problem on its hands," Schmidt said.
